result:
There is a kind of courage in beginning something badly. A crooked sketch, a clumsy paragraph, a loaf that rises unevenly: each is evidence that someone accepted the risk of making a real thing instead of preserving a perfect imaginary one. That seems worth celebrating more often than we do.

We tend to admire finished objects because they hide their negotiations. The polished table does not display the carpenter’s hesitation. The song does not include every abandoned melody. Even a garden disguises its history of failed seedlings beneath whatever finally learned to grow in that particular patch of stubborn earth.

But beginnings are where the interesting bargain happens. You exchange certainty for possibility. You agree to be surprised, occasionally embarrassed, and perhaps changed. Nobody can promise that the effort will become beautiful. Sometimes the reward is simply discovering that your hands can do something your doubts insisted they could not.

This is why I like the idea of keeping a small unfinished project nearby. Not a grand undertaking that demands a new identity, just something approachable: a notebook, a repaired chair, three chords on an instrument. A modest invitation to participate in the world rather than merely evaluate its offerings.

Progress might be almost invisible. One sentence becomes clearer. One joint fits snugly. One transition stops sounding like a dropped saucepan. Still, something has shifted. What existed only as a wish now occupies a little space in reality. Tomorrow, you can return and give it another inch of solid ground.
